# SYSTEM.md contract — rationale

*Generated by bootstrap-system-md. The header in [SYSTEM.md](../SYSTEM.md) states the rules;
this file states why, for humans auditing an agent's edit or disputing one.*

**Contract changelog (replace, don't accrete):** v5 applied 2026-10-15, upgrading a v4-shaped,
unstamped header; scaffolding only, no fact line changed. Gate regenerated from the v5 template
with this repo's configuration carried over.

## How this repo adapts the contract

**Frozen section numbers.** Code, migrations and handoff docs cite `§N` from ~129 places, so the
sections keep their numbers permanently and gaps are allowed; invariants carry `{#inv-slug}` ids
for citations that survive grooming. The contract text itself names sections rather than numbering them.

**Deferred items keep their numbers too.** `§11 item N` is cited from a dozen places, so an item that
moves to `docs/deferred.md` keeps its number and the gap stays in the file.

**Section budgets are a share of the cap, not of the total.** A share-of-total budget tightens every
surviving section the moment one is extracted (after `§4` and `§8` left, `§6` went from 10% to 20% without
a line added). The budget is 25% of the cap rather than the template's 15% because the orientation tier
carries two irreducibly large sections (invariants, agent surfaces) and the contract forbids splitting
orientation content. Recorded here, not silently widened.

**Baselines live in `.slopledger.json`** under `system_md_baselines`, beside the machine-checked
migration triggers, rather than in a separate sidecar.

**The gate's root is the script's parent directory**, never a walk-up: this repo is worked in git
worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/`, and a walk-up validated the main checkout's copy once.


**Why one file.** Split docs fail by disagreeing: a partial update leaves two
files contradicting each other and no reader can tell which is current. The
orientation tier (what/layout/invariants/env/ledgers) therefore stays in one
file. Reference material (entity lifecycles, UI conventions, surface
catalogs) has low contradiction risk and high volume, so it may extract to
`docs/` with an index left behind.

**Why update-after-change (rule 1).** Documentation maintenance follows a
burst-then-taper pattern when it is a separate task. Making the update a
completion criterion of the change itself, performed by whoever holds the
freshest knowledge, is the only version that survives. Note the honest
limit: this bounds staleness to one round of work, not to zero — the file
is accurate at merge boundaries and can drift mid-round.

**Why integrate-don't-append (rule 2).** Agents honor rule 1 by appending
dated paragraphs, because appending never risks breaking someone else's
prose. The file then grows monotonically as a changelog and a reader must
replay history to learn current behavior. Dates in descriptive sections are
the fingerprint of this failure; the gate greps for them.

**Why log lessons (rule 3).** Gotchas are the highest value-per-line
content: they are the failures that recur across agents and models. They
are cheap to write immediately after paying for them and impossible to
reconstruct later.

**Why ledgers shrink (rule 4).** An append-only ledger without eviction is
just bloat with a nicer name. Deferred items without a trigger are read
every session and acted on never. A gotcha whose cause is now enforced by a
test has done its job — it promotes into the invariants section, where it
is checkable, instead of accumulating.

**Why the cap is in bytes.** A line cap is satisfied by widening lines: dense
200-character bullets cost the same tokens as the lines they replaced and
read worse, and the file is rewritten in place to stay "under" a number
that measures nothing. Bytes track tokens closely and cannot be gamed by
reflowing. Lines are still reported, as a readability signal only.

**Why the gate writes the stamp.** Any field a human must remember to update
by hand will drift; a "last revision" line a hundred commits old is worse
than none because it looks maintained. Metadata the gate can derive from
git, the gate writes.

**Why a routing table.** Agents read in slices and always have; the file's
cost is the first-visit tax of finding the slice. Naming the slice per
kind of work cuts the average read more than any extraction, because it
changes the read pattern rather than the file.

**Why the decision record carries rejected alternatives.** When planning,
the fact an agent most often lacks is why the obvious alternative was not
taken. If the repo does not own that, it ends up in an agent's per-user
memory store, which the next agent, model, or vendor does not have.

**Why extraction warnings escalate.** A candidate flagged three audits
running and still present is how an orientation file becomes reference
material without anyone deciding it should. A warning that persists across
two baselines is no longer advice.

**Why caps are earned (rule 5).** Raising the size cap when it is hit is
the document-shaped version of re-baselining past a regression. A cap raise
is legal only after a grooming or extraction pass proved the content
incompressible, with a recorded reason.

**Why anchors, not ordinals.** Section numbers get cited from code, configs,
and handoff docs; a grooming pass renumbers; every citation silently points
at the wrong section. Anchors and rule IDs survive; if numbers are used they
are frozen.

**Why invariants name their enforcement point.** A rule with a test is
checkable; a rule alone is a wish. Pinned invariants are the part of the
file that can be trusted without re-reading the code, and the gate can
verify the named test still exists.

**Why the shims.** The dominant failure of a correct file is that nobody
opens it. Root `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` shims make every auto-loading tool
reach SYSTEM.md without duplicating a single fact.

**Why no secret values.** This file is committed and injected into every
agent's context window. Names and locations only.
